AUSTRIA. A letter from Vienna of the 27th ult., in the Aurembrrg Correspondent, says: þÿ "For the last three days the representatives of England, France and Turkey have regularly assembled at noon in conference with Count tie Buol, and it is stated in a very positive manner that the question of Bolgrad is in the way of a provisional solution, that is to say, that France will adhere to the views ot Austria and of England, who insist on the necessity for the cession of Bolgrad. Baron de Bourqueney has already given explanations on the subject, and a communication on the point has been made to Baron de Ilubner at Paris. This is a new step towards a fresh convocation of a Congress at Paris. Austria and England, however, do not appear to wish to consent to that measure before the other points arising our of the Eastern question, particularly that of the Principalities, shall be more advanced towards a definite solution. We can, therefore, affirm on good authority, that Count Buol has declared to the representative of France that there cannot be any fresh conferences thought of until the organization of the Principalities shall hava been at least drawn up into a project, and approved of by all the Powers who signed the treaty of Paris.

iiUR0(PEAW, From the Illustrated London News, Deer. 13. THE PARIS CONFERENCE. We are still unable to giv< any precise information regarding the pnposed Conference at Paris. The Frenchand Belgian papers continue to discuss the natter in all its bearings, and even to praiounce definitively as to the present poition of the respective Powers, and as to die probable terms of the award. Accoiling to the Journal tics Debuts, Russia, ; France, and Prussia are on one side ; Enghnd, Austria, and Turkey on the other ; wiilo Sardinia, which was said to be at onetime on the side of Russia, is representd as having shown symptoms of joining the opposite party.

Nr. 2. Strange rumours are in circulation also in the Russian and Fusiouist salons regarding an alleged secret understanding between England and Austria, in which France is represented as having no participation whatever. Other reports, equally credible, are afloat, of the discovery by the English Government of an important correspondence said to have been carried on between high personages in Paris and the Court of St. Petersburg relative to a close alliance between France and Russia, and from the present and prospective advantages of which England was to be excluded. More than one foreign Minister accredited to the English Court is said to have recently informed his Government of these facts, as also that copies of the alleged correspondence between Paris and St. Petersburg are actually in the hands of our Government ; and that the feeling entertained by it towards the Emperor of the French is far different from that which existed only twelve months ago. A document addressed by the Russian Government at the latter end of October to all the Powers that signed the Treaty of Paris has been published within the last few days. It was accompanied by a circular requesting the reconvocation of the Paris Conference. This memorandum is an expose of the steps taken by the Cabinet of St. Petersburg with a view to the fulfilment of the Articles 20 and 21 of the Treaty of the BOth of March. Le Sard contains the following remarks on the Bolgrad dispute : þÿ In the beginning of the difficulty France,

which was impartial, leaned to the Russian interpretation ; but for the purpose of conciliation sought for a compromise in combination which it appeared to her ought to satisfy all these angry rivals. Sardinia used the same language as France. Prussia never admitted the interpretation of Austria and England, which she even severely condemned. Opinions, therefore, thus divided : þÿ On the one side Turkey, sustained with violence and the most absolute tone by Austria and England ; and on the other side Russia, supported with firmness by Prussia, and with more reserve by France and Sardinia. Russia then proposed to appeal back to the Congress itself, and formally requested its reassembly. The proposition was equally agreeable to France. Austria, England, and Turkey hastened to decline the offer of Russia þÿ Turkey, in guarded and equivocal language ; Austria, by wrapping its refusal in honeyed forms; and England, with disdainful and insolent arrogance. The attitude of England covered the weakness of Turkey and the hypocrisy of Austria. England placed herself at the head of the resistance, and, at the same time, addressed severe reprimands to the Cabinet of Berlin and the Cabinet of Turin. The latter, however, could not do much. We have already mentioned the tone of these representations of England, couched in a style humiliating, and filled with menace for the two Courts. Prussia was firm ; and England, by way of punishing her, has taken upon herself to support Switzerland in the Neufchatel
question. Everything, therefore, depended upon France and Sardinia. Under these circumstances, the question is incapable of solution.

Lord Chesterfield, in þÿ his þÿ Advice to his þÿSon, justly characterises an absent man as unfit for business or eonver sation. The world is right in this, and 1 would implore every studious youth to forget that he is studious when he enters company. (From the Lonilim Weekly Diapatch, December 14.) Russia is showing her talons in one quarter, and putting out the velvet paw in another. It is all the same tiger dealing. From St. Petersburg, the þÿ Morning þÿPost has advices that 50,000 Russians, commanded by General Bernloff, are ready to march upon the frontiers of Persia at the first call of the Shah. This is plain defiance to England ; a support of one treaty-breaker by another, an announcement that Russia will uphold those who have given us offence in arms, amounting to a declaration of war þÿ a proof that the occupation of Herat by the þÿCzar Persian s vassal is an advance, thought by the Czar worth the risk of a struggle with us, and an announcement that the said Czar thinks he has us at disadvantage, and, after being defeated wherever he could be reached, may now securely oppose us where he believes we cannot find him. The surrender ot Herat to the Persian General, Monrad Chafi, will, no doubt, confirm the Muscovites in their insolent attempt at injustice, and probably pledge the Shah of Persia still further to his course of dishonesty. Meanwhile an expedition is it in the Persian Gulf, and France, well aware, may l ie supposed, of the imminent danger of another great war, offers mediation. Mediation lor the sake of peace by assuring strict justice, will, of course, be welcome, will be kindly and even gratefully accepted The protection of the French Empire dealing with Russia for British interests, and putting points in debate which it behoves our honour and, therefore, our national

life to maintain, is quite another matter. India is worth fighting for, and if it must be kept by the strong hand, we shall do well to begin by keeping invaders from its outposts. 'I his is a world in which we should desire peace and charity, and work for them ; but it is a world in which we cannot always enjoy or ensure them. A noble contention against wrong is the best thing that most of us are born for.

With the name of Submarine Telegraph we have all become familiar : its essential feature consists in the use of an electric conductor, insulated by gutta perehsi, and submerged, instead of being raised on posts in the ordinary manner . With the view of giving strength and protection to this insulated wire both during and subsequent to the subm rsion, it is usual to surround it by iron wires in such a manner as to make it the core or centre of a strong and flexible wire rope. This electric cable, as it i., caiit d, having been once safely deposited at the bottom of the sea, soon imbeds itself, if the bottom he sandy, to such a depth as to be out of reach of auction: or accidents of nnv sort. At three p.m., the proprietor called at my lodgings, and accompanied me to his establisment, which is for the construction of locomotives. The large engine of the works was in operation, and the machine for producing intense cold was placed in the harness and commenced operations. In less than within cury in the thermometer an hour the mer- the machine was reduced from 53 degrees above zero to 24 degrees below that line þÿ that was the lowest figure marked on the scale. I cut an apple in two pieces, and placed it outside the pipes, and in a few minutes it was frozen hard. A copper vessel was placed

alongside of it on the same pipe, and filled with water, which was in a short time converted to solid ice. Water dropped on the pipes was instantly congealed. White frost formed rapidly on the brass pipes and tubes connected with the machine. The machine in its present state is arranged for making a ton of ice at an operation. A square cistern, with a double wall, has the space between the two walls, say about one foot, filled with pulverised charcoal ; inside of the inner wall are six rows, each row containing twelve cast-iron freezers, each capable of holding as much water as will make thirty pounds of ice ; each freezer lias a depth of twelve inches ; and the length is the same as the depth, and the width six inches. A flange or rim of half an inch extends around the four sides of the freezer, and upon this the freezer is suspended by restives or bars running at right angles. The flanges thus arrayed separate the freezers, forming a flue between each of one inch width. A flue of equal thickness extends under the bottom. Tlie steam-engine connects with an airpump which is made to exhaust the atmosphere from these flues, and as soon as a perfect vacuum is produced a current of ether is made to pass through these flues, and continued till all the water in the freezers is converted into 3olid ice. This is the. whole process of refrigeration þÿ simple, yet complete. The expense of making ice by this process is small, and on a large scale can be worked at a. cost not exceeding three

dollars per ton. There is room for improvement in the cast-iron freezers, so that they can be made to discharge the ice with greater facility. This machine is capable of enlargement to the manufacture of hundredsþÿ even of thousands þÿ of tons of ice, and of producing an intensity of cold sufficient for any needed purpose. þÿ Neir York Courier.

A New Calculating Machine. M. Thomas, of Colmar, lias lately made the finishing improvements in the calculating machine, called the arithmometer, at which he lias been working for upwards of thirty years. Pascal and Leibnitz, in the 17th century, and Diderot at a later period, endeavoured to construct a machine which might serve as a substitute for human intelligence in the combination of figures, but I their efforts failed. M. Thomas's arithmometer may be used without the least trouble or possibility of error, not only lor addition, substruction, multiplication, and division, but also for much more complex ' operations, such as the extraction of the square root, involution, the resolution of triangles, &c. A multiplication of eight figures by eight others is made in eighteen seconds ; a division of sixteen figures in 21 seconds ; and in one minute and a quart one can extract the square root of sixteen figures, and also prove the accuracy of the calculation. The arithmometer adapts itself to every sort of combination. As an instance of the wonderful extent of its powers, we may state that it can furnish in a few seconds products amounting to
II A T (' II E T T.

iNr. 4 999, 999,999,999,999,999,999,999,999,999. A marvellous number comparable to the infinite multitude of stars which stud the firmament, or the particles of dust which tloat in the atmosphere. The working ot this instrument is, however, most simple. To raise or lower a nut screw, to turn a winch a few times, and, by means of a button, to slide oil a metal plate from left to right, or from right to left, is the whole secret. The arithmometer is moreover a simple instrument, of very little volume and easily portable. It is already used in many great financial establishments, where considerable economy is realised by its employment. It. will soon be considered as indispensable, and lie as generally used as in a clock, which was formerly to be seen palaces, and is now in every cottage. þÿ Paris Moniteur.

The African Discoverer. þÿ The Rev. Dr Livingstone, who is daily expected in London, arrived at Marseilles Irom Tunis on the (5th instant, and was then in good health. Mis left arm is, however, broken and partly useless, it having been torn by a lion. When he was taken on hoard her Majesty's ship the Frolic, on the Mozambique coast, he had great difficulty in speaking a sentence of English, having disused it so long while travelling in Africa, lie had with him a native from the interior of Africa. This man, when lie got to the Mauritius, was so excited with the steamers and various wonders of civilisation that lie went mail, and jumped into the sea and was drowned. Dr. Livingstone has been absent from England seventeen years, lie ( ross<M I the great African continent almost in the centre, from west to east, has been where no civilised being has ever been before, and has made many notable discoveries of great value, lie travelled in the twofold character of missionary and physician, having obtained a medical diploma, lie is rather a short man, with a pleasing and serious countenance, which betokens the most determined resolution.

Sir, As you acknowledge a dullness of perception with regard to the conclusion arrived at by the Burgher Council concerning the election in Frederiksted and the objections started by Mr. Newton against the validity of this election, I will with your permission try to clear the evidently confused ideas entertained on this subject, a task which I think you yourself came very near performing when you

. C R 0 I X A y I, & . refered complainants to 8 of the Ordinance of May 9tli 1855, and whicli you said would also have completed simply by applying this and know- to Mr. Newton's cuse. Omitting ing the law, it is you, 1 should think, who fell into "confusion worse counfonded." Regarding the printed list, which Mr. Newton asserts is correct, but which is incorrect, it seems sufficient to state, that it was not the list which according to 7 of the Ordinance was prepared by the Council, sent to the director of the elections and exhibited in the Courthouse. Nor was it either authorized by the Council, or printed by their order. The words in the minutes quoted " and these to be printed" form no part of the Council's resolution, and when seen in the draft, were objected to by the member who revised it before printing ; nevertheless, these words were not withmember of the Council. Consequently, the held from the minutes, and surprised every ' Treasurer and his clerk were not blamed by the majority of the Council for having done as lie was directed," and the Chairman was perfectly right in laying the blame for the error on the officials of the Council. This printed list not agreeing with the exhibited and authentic written list, it could certainly not he acknowledged as valid by the electoral Committee, nor could the disputed point he legally settled in the manner suggested nature in your editorial. The lists can he corrected only hv acting according to 8 of the Ordinance ; and when the printed list is an exact

and certified copy of the authentic list, it matters little whether objections and reclamations are preferred to the one or the other ; but when such is not the case, as in this instance, the action must of course be taken against the authentic list. If Mr. Newton was ignorant of this. although þÿ it is said that the Director of the Poll had the extreme obligeance to inform him in good time of the omission of his name, þÿ he must onlv blame himself. It is absurd to expect or demand that the election should be held invalid because of his ignorance of the law ; it is more absurd still, to insinuate personal motives in the Director or Directors of the Poll, as if it could be thought worth their while indeed to plot for the exclusion of Mr. Newton from the Burgher Council. The annual list, as ordered by the law, will, notwithstanding all possible diligence in the Council and their officials, rarely escape having errors; it is therefore ordained to he publicly exhibited and open for corrections no within a stated time. This having elapsed, more corrections enn he affected, and the electoral Committee has within the following 8 days to decide in a public meeting, held for that purpose, upon the objections which have come forward. Now, the printed lists weie not thus exhibited either in Christiausted or in Frederiksted, they were not even handed to the directors in legally sufficient time for being exhibited, for, although bearing the same date as the authentic, lists, of which they were in-

tended to be copies, yet they were only printed after these had been sent to the directors Both of these functionaries concluded at once, that these incorrect copies could not supersede the authentic lists, and the director at Frederiksted informed the Secretary of the Council thereof. Neither Mr. Newton nor any body else having made any reclamation against the. authentic list within the prescribed tune, there was of course no occasion to hold a public meeting for deciding thereon, and of there conse- quently at all legal alteration was no in the possibility list before the making next any annual lists are composed. On the day of election there appeared at the poll five persons desiring to vote for Mr Newton, and on being informed by the Committee that he was not on the list as eligible, two of I them voted for other candidates, and three declined voting at all. These, Sir, are the simple facts regarding this much agitated question, and it is surpriscil should have pronounced the election ing, not that the majority in the Burgher of Coun- Mr. Elliott valid, but rather that you, Mr. Editor and Mr. Newton, as also the minority in the Council should have entertained auy doubt as to the correctness of this decision. 1 am, Sir, your obdt. servt HEILBUTH Prosperity, January llth 1857.

From the St. Thomas " Tidende," January 7. To the Editor of the " St. Thorn® Tidende." Sir, þÿ In your last publication we observed your remarks respecting our local Post-office, in connection with which we request you will insert the following : þÿ At 3 o'clock on the 2nd instant a letter for us from Puerto Cabello was brought to the store by a carrier of the Post-office ; it happened that at the moment no one was present to pay the demanded 4 cents upon it, and the let ter was taken away ; it was brought hack on the 3rd inst , only at 1 o'clock. It lias ever been a custom of the carriers since the establishment of the office, to deliver the letters and call afterwards for the amount charged, which we have always p.iid. Had our letter been left in the store as usual, we should not now have to feel mortified, for we could have replied to a very important commu nication by Captain Todd, who left here same day for LaGuayra. This is not only an annoyance but may eventually he a loss to us, as other parties had full time to answer their correspondence and we had not. Can circumstances like this be construed into one of the " facilities offered to the public," of which the Postmaster treats in his advertisement of November last ? This case is not the first of like we have to complain of ; on one occasion we saw two letters from Curasao delivered at 9 a.m., when we received ours at 1 p.m., Where, Mr Editor, are we to look for redress ! Every body feels how sorely this Post-office regulation affects the feelings of this communi-

ty, and which clogs the wheels of the commerce of the island. It has been stated, with what truth we do not know, that the office was established to give employment to an old meritorious officer of the Military. If this is really the case we are firmly inclined to believe that if an application in his behalf were being made to the mercantile community of the island, they would cheerfully step forward and provide for him an equivalent to any emolument which the office may yield him, if, by that means, we could succeed in getting rid of the Post-office regulation, such as now exercised, and in our opinion, contrary to the law on foreign letters by foreign vessels. RIDGWAY, BUHL & Co. St. Thomas, Jan. 6, 1857.

The President is preparing a special message, which will be sent to Congress in a lew days, asking an appropriation to aid in laying the cable between Newfoundland and Ireland, or rather to give the company the same encouragement that England has. It has, since its introduction into this country, proved itself well adapted to our geographical range ol Indian corn. It is of easy culture, being similar to that of maize or brown corn, but will prosper in a much poorer soil. FOREIGN INTELLIGENT !E. Paris, Friday, C p.m. An Italian gentleman, who left Naples on the 7th inst., has given me a curious, and I believe not an untruthful, picture of the state ol that couutry at the present moment. I may premise that my informant is a Neapolitan ; he is not a refugee, he has not been mixed up in politics; ho merely paid a visit recently to his native country alter a lengthened abseuce, and lie now returns, not to France or England, but to another more distant couutry, where he is engaged in business. During bis stay in Naples bo visited the provinces. lie comes, therefore, lull of information, which is of value inasmuch as it proceeds from a person quite capable of forming an opinion on the real state of the country, and of expressing it impartially. I give you a summary of a long conversation. It would appear, according to his account, that the Neapolitan revolution continues to be directed by (I omit tbe names of the persons for obvious reasons), and the other chiefs of that party They are uo longer either Bourbonites or Unitarians þÿ they are Federalists. They prevent the explosion of the revolution, for they do not wish to trust to the chances of street fighting the moral revolution which is already effected. In truth, the Neapolitans are no longer the gay and noisy people travellers knew them to be not long ago. They are become serious, speak little and in a low voice, hut whatever they do say they say it without fear. The terror which hung over them no longer exists ; you hear them speak of the

incompatibility of Ferdinand II , of the Constitution, and of liberty, without apprelieusiou or disguise. One would suppose they are anxious to go to prison, but the police dare not gratify t heir wish. They seem to wi>h that the police should commit excesses ; but Biauchini docs not venture, or does not wish, to gratify them. Bianchiui is respected and honoured as an honest man; his police are tolerant, and even civil. The police are now divided into two parts þÿ the old and the new, and these last detest the excises of the agents of Mazza Neither Morbell, nor Catnpagna, nor Creffi is now seen in the streets. They have disappeared, and are afraid to show themselves in public. The king earnestly desires to get rid of Bianehini, whom lie detests, but he dare not brave public opinion so far as to remove him. Much distress exists. Since the departure of the French and English Ambassadors thousands of strangers have left Naples, and none arrive. Hotels and houses arc empty, and several shops in the Toledo arc shut up. Commercial affairs are at a st ind, and distress is on the increase. The moral revolution is very nearly complete ; except a handful of Lizznoni who inhabit the Quarter St. Lucia, the whole population detest the King, his Government, and his system. The L azz noni of the other quarters of the city, who arc in part armed, arc for the deposition of the Bourbons and for liberty. An employe under Government is designated by the epithet of Pagnoliish. þÿ that is, a poor wretch who cares for nothing except

for the bread he earns. The Swiss have, as it were, disappeared ; shut up in the castles, with the mission of exterminating the people and bombarding the city, hardly one is ever seen abroad, and the few families who hitherto received the Swiss officers into their houses now ex dude them. The Swiss at Naples are now pretty much on the same footing with respect to the inhabitants as the Austrian at Milan. Tlio troops are discontented, and since the King lias nominated his 24 new generals the discontent of the officers has increased. The King fears the native troops and despises them. Foreign papers and proclamations are circulated everywhere. At Naples conversation is very monotonous. If you happen to see two or throe persons speak together iti an eating-house you may be sure it is to this effect þÿ "Ferdinand II., impossible ; bis son, we don't know him, but they say he is brought up by the priests and is half an idiot. What wo want is a Constitution like that of Belgium." It is a folly to sit down at home in " a slovenly state, consoled with the remark, Nobody will call to-day." Should somebody call we are in no plight to receive them, and otherwise it is an injury to the character to allow slovenly habits to control us even when we are unseen. Commands should never be given in a commanding tone. A real gentleman requests, he does not command We are not to assume so much importance, whatever our station, as to give orders in the " imperative mood," nor are we ever justified in thrusting the consciousness of servitude on any one. The blunder of commanding sternly is most frequently committed by those who have themselves but just escaped servitude, and we should not exhibit to others a weakness so unbecoming. Control of Temper. þÿ It is very unbecoming to exhibit petulance, or angry feeling, though it is indulged in so largely in almost every circle. The true gentleman does not suffer his countenance to be easily ruffled ; and we only look paltry when we suffer temper to hurry us into ill-judged expressions of feeling. ' He that is soon angry dealeth foolishly." Conversation ranks the highest among social enjoyments. To converse well requires extensive knowledge, elegance of manner, command of temper, and a desire to please, lie who cannot converse to the profit of the company, must listen for the profit himself; though

no one need preserve a stolid silence from excessive bashfulncss or conscious inability. The smallest remark may be well-timed and elegantly uttered ; the lightest observation properly pointed and emphasised, and the most trivial question put with modesty, grace, and elegance of expression. Yet, in middle-class society, how little really good conversation do we bear ? How frequently personalities creep in ; how one gives way to undue warmth when his religious and political principles are assailed ; how another jests and puns upon the most serious subjects ; or a third plays the pedant by the use of a string of technicalities, which be himself scarcely understands, to adorn his shallow learning and his imperfect judgment. NF.WS FROM AUSTRALIA. From the New York Herald. The intelligence generally is of a very satisfactory nature. Fresh discoveries of gold had been made ; silver, copper, tin, iron, slate and marble had also been found, from which the most sanguine expectations were entertained. Trade was brisk, the colony tranquil and prosperous, and the inhabitants generally contented and happy.

The Melbourne Herald of 12th of September, has the following summary of events : þÿ In Victoria, the gold fields þÿ which every experiment and inquiry shows to be inexhaustible þÿ are yielding a larger produce, and new ones are being opened in all directions. Quartz mining proves to be lucrative in skilful hands, possessed of capital ; and this being ascertained, a new complexion will be given to mining enterprise. The individual digger, or small companies of industrious men, relying almost exclusively on brawny arms and stubborn resolution, will commence with the pick and spade, and such other appliances as humble means will command, t hey will, in many instances, create capital, and that very quickly. An investment in a quartz crushing partnership under the cost book system then presents itselt, and the judicious adventurer finds himsell on the road to competence, with little further trouble than that implied in vigilance and personal superintendence. Recent discoveries have been reported both of tin and silver, and a careful exploration is being made of a coal mine, to which we alluded in our last summary, said to have been found on the shores of Port Philip. Quarries of slate and marble have been pointed out, and last, though not least, of all these additions to our wealth and comfort a bank of codfish has been sprung, so to speak, in the neighborhood of þÿKing Island. s þÿHaas S s trait. Our returns of all kinds show a state of real prosperity and healthy trade.

The gold yield gives a total for this year of 1 ,804,014 oz. The escort from the Ovetis arrived in town on Monday evening with 11,200 oz. Returns since our last summary have been kept up to their average, although some allowance might be made for the license of general election time at the diggings. Quartz crushing operations were being extended, and no doubt could exist of the ultimate success of such a system. The price of gold remains at £3 15s. 3d. per ounce. Entries were passed at the Customs on the 12th of September for 33,0 17 ounces for London. EUROPEAN.

From the London Times, December 15. One relic of the many expeditions which have been despatched in search of Sir John Fraki.in and his companions has at length reached our shores in the shape of the stout old Resolute. On Friday afternoon, at half-past 2, in the midst of a violent storm of rain, lightning, and thunder, she was anchored at Spithead. The story of the abandonment of this ship and of so many others in the Arctic ice is too fresh in the public recollection to need repetition here. Suffice it to say, that she got adrift from the frozen regions in which she had been abandoned, that she drifted about a thousand miles, that she was then seen and hoarded by the officers and crew of the American whaling-ship George Henry, and by them conveyed into a United þÿStates port. On the part of Congress a very graceful act followed. It was resolved by the Senate and House of Representatives to appropriate a sum of 40,00(1 dollars to the purchase of the Resolute, with all the | armament, equipment, and property on hoard. This done, the ship was to be moved into one of the Navy-yards of the United States, there to be fully repaired and equipped, and to be despatched to England as an offering of goodwill and friendship from the United States to Great Britain. All has been done as resolved. On the 13th of November the Resolute com- I inenced her homeward voyage, and on the 12th of December she reached Spithead. j She arrived under American colours, but as soon as she let go her anchors the Eng-

lish was run up alongside of the American ensign. Every care has been taken that ingenuity could devise to replace every- I thing on hoard in the same condition as j when the ship was abandoned by the Arctic i adventurers. The Resolute, indeed, is, in all probability, as sound and seaworthy in i every respect as when she sailed away from the British shores upon her last Polar adventure. We rejoice to hear that II tit Majk.ty will, by an act of singular grace and courtesy, evince her sense of the good feeling of the United States. If we are not misinformed, she will to-morrow pay a visit to the Resolute.

SWEDEN. At the opening of the Swedish Diet King Oscar announced in very noble language that a bill would be presented in the course of the session for the establishment of freedom of religious worship in the kingdom. The text of that measure has just been published, and it proves how strong religious prejudices must still he iu Sweden, since notwithstanding the good intentions of the Sovereign and the spirit of the constitution, the Government has only ventured to propose enactments of a very limited character, and which do not by any means reach the standard which the þÿKing language s had led people to expect. The following is an analysis of the principal provisions of the bill : þÿ Art. 1 revokes the clauses and enactments of the Penal Code relative to the penalties attached to departure from the true Evangelical doctrine, and the profession of another faith These penalties were nothing less than exile and confiscation, and the persons who left the Swedish Chueh almost in every case merely became Protestants of another denomination. Every Swede, however, who leaves the national Swedish Church is obliged to make a formal declaration to that effect in the registers of his parish. Art. 2 revokes the enactments of the same code which entail the penalty of exile for the propagation of erroneous doctrines, and changes the punishment for that offences into a tine, varying from 68f. to 460f., or imprisonment for from one to 12 months. Art. 3 proposes that whoever shall seek bv persuasion,

threats, or other illicit means to lead to apostasy from the Swedish Church shall be liable to a line of from 70f. to 440f., and for each repetition of the offence to imprisonment for from two to 12 months. Art. 4 states that children born before their parents have changed arc to he brought up in the doctrines of the Swedish Church, and the municipal councillors are ordered to see that this prescription is carefully carried out. Art. 5 states that no one can, in consequence of his religious profession, be released from the observance of all the laws iu vigour in the kingdom. Art. (i allows members of the Swedish Church to hold religious meetings iu private houses, provided nothing takes place calculated to destroy public order. Iu every meeting for the purpose of religious worship at which a clergyman does not officiate entrance cannot he refused either to the clergyman of the parish or to the public function aries of the neighbourhood ; and these latter can, in case of illegality or disorder, dissolve the meetings. No such meetings, however, can in any case take place, unless by a special permission, under the penalty of a tine from G8f. to 1/iOf., for the person lending his house, and of 1 If. for each person present þÿ

THE WISE MAN AND THE F< >OL. What is the difference between the wise man and the fool? The one is ever learning, the other never. You bray the fool seven times in a mortar, lie comes out a fool still. The wise man needs no braying; he saves you the trouble. The fool has eyes, hut sees not; ears, hut hears not; understanding, of a sort, but lets it lie fallow. The wise man has his eyes and ears always open: no fact so trivial as to he beneath his regard ; and what lie sees and hears, he digests with his understanding ; thus ever adding to his knowledge and his wisdom. The tool sees the timbers of his house rotting day by day, one brick falling after another; the ground falling awaj' from the foundation inch by inch ; he sees, hut takes no note: if warned, lie shrugs his shoulders and says, he doubts not it will last his time. The wise man employs a builder to apply a remedy ; or, if the evil he past cure, pulls his house down and builds a stronger. The fool puts off till to-morrow what should he done to-day. þÿ Time þÿenough, is his motto. The wise man takes time by the forelock : þÿ No time like the present," is his.

J OlIR DEALINGS WITH ENGLAND. i The progress of civilization, and the humanizing tendency of knowledge are bringing about, at this moment, two changes in the relations between this country and England, which are of the highest moment to the world tit large. One of these is the At lantic telegraph, a noble institution, if ever there was one, and one eminently deserving not only private patronage, which is the best, but likewise public, which is the worst. We are glad to hear that President Pierce is disposed to meet the Telegraph company half way, and send a message to Congress recommending that the United States award to the enterprise the same encouragement as it has received from the government of England. The British government have agreed to pay $70,000 per annum for the right of sending messages over the wire, and have further lent two steamers to assist in laying the wire. The United States have already vouchsafed the services of the steamer

Arctic; and they can well afford to make the balance of their contribution equal to that of England. At the same time, while this is being done, and for the very reason that it is done under the sanction of the

made, so to speak, an international one, it is eminently desirable that the terms on which it is started be such that no complaint can ever arise out of them, and that no Americans shall ever regret that the company was successful. That, we are bound to say, might be the case at any moment, in the event of a war between this country and England. So long as G reat Britain holds the termini of the wire, on either side of the Atlantic, with power to prohibit the United States from using it, and to enforce a monopoly of ocean telegraphing for herself, the telegraph will be a benefit largely mixed with danger for this country. It might be used tor our detriment ; it certainly could not be used tor our good, in the case we have supposed. If, indeed, the government of England, by special treaty, were to declare the telegraph wire and stations neutral, so that neither they nor the persons employed on them should participate in any war that might take place between England and this country, then the United States might judiciously set their national stamp Such scheme ; but hardly otherwise. on the an exemption as we speak ot would not be without precedent. From tho Illustrated London Xo\v«, December 27 THE WAR WITH PERSIA. The next Overland Mail will, no doubt, bring some news from the Persian Gulf regarding the expedition sent from Bombay. Meanwhile we have all manner of rumours as to what is going on in Persia and the neighbouring Russian provinces. A Polish correspondent of the Avg>burg Gazette writes that the Russians have long been | preparing for the outbreak of war between England and Persia. The garrison of Astrakhan has been strengthened, and the Cossacks in the neighbourhood of that city have received a new commander in the person of Lieutenant- General Krassnik ; but the reports relative to the concentration of troops, which are to lu; conveyed by þÿ the flotilla of the Caspian Sea to Astrabad, are totally þÿunfounded. The Orenburg corps, of which so much has recently been said, consists of the 23rd infantry division and of the Orenburg battalions of the line, but it is too weak to be sent on an expedition to Persia. The distance is so enormous i that there can lie no question of a reinforcement being sent from Southern Russia. T he principal force of Russia in Asia is in the Caucasus and on the Araxes, and, it her troops should enter Persia, it would probably be by way of the province of Azcrbijan. A private letter from Astrakhan of the 15th of November, published in the Monitcur de la Finite, gives some details relative to the situation of the Russian forces on the Caspian Sea. No portion of the Russian army had entered

the Persian territory, nor was war considered imminent. A commission, composed of a Colonel of the staff, of a Lieutenant-Colonel of Engineers, and of a superior officer of infantry, had been sent from the Russian head-quarters to visit Mazanderan, a province of Persia on the coast of the Caspian Sea, to examine pas sages and prepare maps. It appears that in case of hostilities between Great Britain and Persia, the province of Mazanderan would afford an important strategical position. Troops might be concentrated at Balfroueh, the principal town of the province, at Meehedi-Ser, Astrabad, Ascharf, and Feesh-Abad. Independently of these military dispositions, the defile of the Caspian Gates and that of Kotuis, might be effectually occupied. It is through

these points that the centre of the kingdom of Persia may he reached. Flic concentration in Mazanderan of the Russian army in the provinces of the Caspian Sea, now consisting of 50,000 men, would, it is said, render the operations of the British army extremely difficult, as it would be constantly menaced in its flank or its rear by the army in .Mazanderan. The writer of this letter believes that for these reasons the differences between Great Britain and Persia will be settled amicably. Acccording to the Constantinople correspondent of the Tried. Zeitung, the demands þÿ made bv England on Persia are : þÿ 1. Revision of the treaties between the two Powers. 2. Evacuation of Herat. 3. Permission to establish þÿ factories in the Persian Gulf. 4. Railroad concessions to English companies. The Imaum of Muscat, who is with England, refuses to pay any more tribute to Persia. A letter from Erzeroum, dated November 18, states that an extraordinary courier from Persia had brought the news that Herat had fallen on the 25th October into the hands of the Persian army after a very sanguinary conflict. The news appears likely to be true, but it is the cholera and hunger which have obliged the garrison of Herat to surrender, and not the valour of their assailants.

FRANCE. To-day the Emperor passed a grand review in the Place du Carrousel for the delectation of Prince Frederick William of Prussia. Nine regiments of the line and three battalions of Foot Chasseurs were drawn up on the ground in battle array, and divided into two divisions of two brigades each The Emperor ceded the place next the troops to the Prussian Prince, who wore his Colonel's uniform and the Grand Cordon of the Legion of Honour, while the Emperor wore the Cordon of a Prussian order. Marshals Vuillant, Magnan, Paraguay d'Hilliers, and Canrobert were among his Majestv's suite. Most of the regiments present at this review wore the Crimean medal. þÿImitation. There are few who can resist the tendency of human nature to imitate. Let one young man of a group take to swearing, and the rest of his juvenile friends will immediately follow the practice. 1 have known the style of conversation, in a complete circle of acquaintance, to be changed by the peculiarities of one of its members ; impressed with those peculiarities, the rest have set about apeing him to the best of their poor abilities, and succeeded in making themselves ridiculous. There þÿ is a passage in Shirley þÿIlibberd s story of þÿCloribel, which we would offer here as a motto for every sensible youth, þÿ Be thyself and none other, and we will love thee, whatþÿsoe er thou þÿart. Imitate the perfections, not the vices, the excellencies rather than the blemishes of a man ; hut preserve your individuality as far as you are able. Introductions should he performed with great grace and judgment. Be careful, too, whom you introduce ; I have seen more than one friend ruined by an ill-judged introduction. It is a common blunder to introduce persons in the street. If you meet an aquaintance when you have a friend on your arm, how and pass on with a þÿ good þÿday, or similar greeting, unless there he special reasons for halting. We only reprobate street introductions as a rule. There arc exceptions to that as to all rules. We have once or twice been mortified by a sudden introduction on a door-step. Consider time and place. It is necessary, too, in most cases, to ask permission of a friend before

you introduce him to another; and a lady must he introduced to a gentleman, not a gentleman to a lady. Invitations. þÿ The writer from whom we have already quoted, says on this subject, þÿ When you ask a person to dinner, let it, if possible, he done a week or ten days in advance ; because, to ask a person only' a day or two days before, looks as if you had been disappointed of somebody else, and had asked him ns a mere stop-gap. A short invitation is only allowable for off-hand parties, or with strangers who are passing through a town. þÿ When you invite a person to dinner, or any other party at your house, specify only one day. þÿDon say t you will he glad to see him on either of two days, as Tuesday or Wednesday next. And why? Because this person may not wish to dine with or visit you at all ; and so far from a choice of days being thought an act of kindness, it may he considered one of servility, if not rudeness. Always state only one day ; and let the invitation, like the answer, he unequivocal. þÿ Invitations for several weeks in advance are almost as had as invitations for alternate days ; because long invitations convey the impression that the invitcr is desperately ill off for guests, and wishes to insure a number at all risks. The person invited is also apt to feel that it is not his pleasure or convenience that is consulted ; and to raise a feeling of this kind is anything hut consistent with true politeness. þÿ The receiver of an invitation has a duty to perform as well as its giver. þÿ on him to say yes nr no at once not to allow a It is incumbent

post or a day to elapse before answering. The reason is obvious : a delay on his part looks as if he were waiting for a better invitation before he made up his mind. Not to send a speedy rejily, therefore, is one of the worst pieces of breeding of which a man can he guilty. It is also not using the inviter well ; for a dinner-party usually consists only of a certain number, and if you cannot accept the invitation, say so, in order that time may be allowed to invite another person in your place. Let the answer also he distinct, no uncertainty is allowable ; and if the invitation be accepted, let it be kept. þÿ The answer to an invitation should he directed to the lady of the þÿhouse. An invitation may be refused, or you cannot have a will of your own; but the refusal should be couched in the kindest, briefest, and most polite terms. Jesting. þÿ Never make sport of the failings or peculiarities of another. Such things are

If a joke is levelled at you, do not suffer your temper to get the worse of you, but join in the laugh good-temperedly, and the jester will he beaten by your good humour. Jests are not always vulgar, and are allowable with familiar friends, hut never with strangers, and always without personality or ill feeling.

Ladies. þÿ Some coxcombs pride themselves on their female acquaintance, and talk freely to their convivial friends of them. This is a detestable vice, and at once stamps a man as base and cowardly. Others affect a contempt for women, and treat them slightingly. Such conduct is at the least unmanly, and generally springs from a puffed-up conceit. Deference is due to woman in every station of society, and is a characteristic of the true gentleman. Leaving Company. þÿ French leave is the fashion now-a-days in good society, and we should hope may continue so. By this method you slip out, shake hands quietly with the host and hostess, and the party goes on undisturbed ; otherwise the movement of one is frequently the signal for the movement of another, and the party is broken up prematurely. I have seen, in homely assemblies, a sedate matron retire to dress, and re-appear with bonnet and shawl on to shake hands with the whole company. Nothing can be more vulgar, or detrimental to the life of a party, however unpretending its character. Letters. þÿ To answer letters promptly, explicitly, and briefly, is a duty incumbent on every person receiving one. 1 have known persons leave letters for weeks unanswered, with the consoling remark, þÿ Ah ! þÿthere s Soþÿand-so letter, s I must answer that in a day or þÿtwo. What should we think if we spoke to a man and did not get a reply for a fortnight, and yet to delay answering a letter is as unbecoming. In addressing persons, be particu-

lar to assign them their proper rank, and make no difference in your mode of address, even if a quarrel takes place, unless the intimacy is formally broken off, when the þÿ Dear þÿSir must relapse into the þÿ þÿSir again. 1 have once or twice been annoyed by a person who had always addressed me þÿ Dear þÿSir, address me as þÿ Sir," after we had had a slight difference. I always knew then I had a paltry mind to deal with, and acted accordingly. Impertinent and insolent letter are best not answered. Of all things keep clear of a paper war; it is a conflict in which the gentleman is sure to be flogged out of you. Long letters are indulged in very much by the uncultivated, but brevity in writing is the rule for a gentleman. Invitations by letter should proceed from the lady of the house, and replies should be addressed to her in return. I would recommend adherence to this rule, even in little invitations to tea passing from one friend to another. They give wives their proper place and importance, and that is essential to decorum, comfort, and propriety. Mourning. þÿ In calling on a friend who is in distress, put on a little mourning also, or at least go in no flashy attire. If your correspondent seals his letters with black, seal yours to him with black also. Mysteriousness. þÿ Never be dark or mysterious. If propriety does not allow you to say a thing outright, do not allude to it at all. A gentleman or lady always attends to those old but excellent mottoes, þÿ Mind your own busi-

þÿness, and þÿ A still tongue makes a wise þÿhead. Punctuality is one of the characteristics of politeness. He who does not keep his appointments promptly is unfit for the society of gentlemen, and will soon find himself" shut out from it.

Punning is of late years very much indulged in. It is not altogether objectionable, but is liable to become so ; for punsters, like mad dogs, when once started, run on till they are exhausted. Punning, too, is the lowest species wit, and unless puns are most hap- of pily pointed, and free from all personal allusion, they are silly and contemptible. If you pun, do not laugh at your own joke. Purse-pride is to be seen everywhere, and is always an evidence of weakness and vulgarity. Make no exhibition of your means ; and if misfortune befal any of your friends, be still more careful not to display before them your superior fortune. Many a heart has been rankled by conduct of this sort, which prevails largely amongst the members of families.

Hongkong, Nov. 15. The London mail of the 10th September arrived here on the 2d instant, per steamer Singapore, and we yesterday received, via Calcutta, telegraphic news from London to the 26th September. The Singapore leaves at 2 p.m. do-day with the outward mail, which is of more than usual political importance. Unexpected events have occurred at Canton, j which has been partially bombarded by the Bri- j tish fleet, and trade is entirely suspended, most : of the foreign residents having retired to Hong- | kong and Macao, with their books and treasure, j The supercilious and insolent bearing of the j Chinese officials towards the British Government and people has long required a check, which, | being delayed, at last emboldened the Viceroy to iusult our flag and refuse all apology for the outrage. The more immediate cause of offence is as i follows; þÿ A lorcha, possessing a colonial register, ) and entitled, therefore, to bear the British flag , and claim its protection, was anchored off Canton i on the bth of October, when a party of Imperial | soldiers boarded the vessel, seized 12 Chinese of the crew, whom they sent on shore, and, hauling down the Union Jack, retained possession of the lorcha. The master, an Englishman, applied to Her Britannic þÿMajesty Consul, s who forthwith went on board. On remonstrating with the Mandarin officer, he was insulted and even threatened with violeuce. The Consul then addressed the Viceroy, detailing the tacts and requiring immediate redress, which so far from '

being granted was distinctly refused, the Viceroy appearing determined to defend the act. Mr. Consul Farkes then communicated with Her 1 þÿMajesty s Plenipotentiary here, and 24 hours were granted to the Viceroy Ych to apologize for the iusult to our flag and Consul. Such an apology not being forthcoming, Mr. Farkes on the 221 October publicly notified that the task of exacting satisfaction had devolved on Her þÿMajesty s naval officers. Meantime his Excellency Rear-Admiral Sir Michael Seymour had proceeded to Canton, taking with him all the fleet except Her þÿMajesty ship s Winchester; the boats and spare force from that vessel, however, , joined the expedition. The Admiral demanded redress and apology I and a salute of 21 guns to the British flug, and gave the Viceroy 24 hours further to consider I the course he was pursuing, ample warning being given that should he still reluse compliance coercive measures would be adopted. Yeh, however, made no satisfactory overtures, j and the tone of his communications was anything but apologetic. But one course, therefore, remained for Sir Michael Seymour, and on the 24th of October all save one of the river forts at and about Can- j ton were taken by our seamen and marines I without loss, the Chinese offering but a poor resistance. The guns were spiked, to the number of 170, and some of the forts were burnt, while others were held by our marines and a detachment of the Royal Artillery, sent up from this place, under the command of Captain Rotfon,

R.A. Some days were then allowed to elapse, and every opportunity was given to Yeh to arrange matters, if so inclined. The Viceroy, however, remained obstinate, and the usual Chinese policy was resorted to. 12 men, with chains round their necks, were sent to the Consulate ( not on board the lorcha, as had been demanded ), purporting to be the same as were taken from the vessel. They were, however, wretches of the lowest class, evidently dragged from prison, and were, of course, sent back at once, and, all attempts at negotiation having failed, on the 27th

Quarrels are lowering to the parties en- | of October the Encounter steamer, Captain þÿO Callaghan,opened fire on the city wall and the þÿViceroy spalace, the Royal Artillery cooperating from one of the captured forts. Her þÿMajesty steamer s Barracouta, Captain Fortescue. steamed up a branch of the river, and from a distance of 3,200 yards threw shot and shell into the forts on the heights. A breacli having been effected in the city wall, it was stormed on the 20th of October by the marines and sailors, led by Commodore Elliot The breach was carried after some resistance, and the þÿViceroy p s alace was also taken possession of and visited by Sir M. Seymour. Our troops were withdrawn before dark, our loss for the day amounting to only three killed and 1 1 wounded. Further attempts at negotiation were then made, hut all proved fruitless. On the 3d and 4th November the old city was shelled, and on the 6th Her þÿMajesty s steamer Barracouta engaged and destroyed a fleet of 23 war junks, anchored in line off the small fort not previously taken. The Barracouta had hot work, anil received no less than SO shot in her hull amt rigging. The Chinese stood to their guns better than usual- This lort was also taken by tlm boats of the Calcutta. Our loss ammouuted to three killed and two wounded. His Excellency having previously reconnoitred the Bogue Forts, at the entrance of the Canton river, they were taken on the 12th instant, after some fighting, by which we lost two killed and four wounded,

one of the latter a midshipman. The ships of war in the Canton river are : þÿ Sailing vessels. þÿ Calcutta, flag, SO; Sybille. broad pendant, 44; Nankin, 50; Comus, 14. þÿSteamers. Niger, 14 ; Encounter, 14; Barracouta, 0; Sampson, 6; Hornet, 17; Coromandel, 3. His Excellency Sir M. Seymour, in whosp hands the whole affair rested, lias gained tlm respect and administration of all the British subjects here. The patience and humanity ho has displayed, and the unflinching determination with which he acts, have inspired the greatest confidence Throughout the whole matter the community have been kept fully informed on all points needful for them to know. The factories have been strongly and efficiently guarded, and no precautions which care and foresight could suggest have been wanting to assure the minds of those most interested Such an opportunity has not before offered for revising our treaty with China and establishing our relations on a footing which may guard against the recurrence of such acts as those which have now brought us into hostile collision with the Chinese. It is needless to point out the position of va-t importance to the revenues of Great Britain and India which the commerce of China holds, or the great extension of which it is capable, were our means of intercourse extended, as they are with other nations. Now is the time for an Kmbasssy to Pekin, having at its head some one of that high character a tad standing fitted to represent Her Majesty in such a mission ; hut for this we must look at home.

The views of i nr home Government will ho anxiously expected here, and we trust that the high influence of the press, as well as of all connected with Chinese affairs, will he exerted in pressing the matter on the attention of Her þÿMajesty G s overnment. V ulg akities. þÿ We often have inward promptings of the vulgarity of our actions ; there is a sort of instinctive propriety in all of us, and whenever we heed these monitions from within, we are pretty sure to be in the right. If you have a doubt at any time of the propriety of an action, let instinct guide you, and you are safe. I have observed that it is very common for persons to talk very loud when in conversation with foreigners, as if increase of noise would compensate for difficulties of mutual understanding. In omnibus and railway travelling there is a good deal of bawling, treading on toes, thrusting of elbows into sides, crushing, crowding, and running to and fro In the midst of all this confusion the gentleman, punctual to time, walks with ease ro his place, takes his seat without hurry or noise, and, in securing his own comfort, regards the comfort of others by a spirit of conciliating accommodation The other day, while riding in an omnibus, I was much annoyed, as were others of the passengers, by two females, (I regret 1 cannot say ladies), who sat with heads protruding from the windows, shouting and passing pleasantries to some acquaintance on the pathway. Rudeness of any kind on such occasions causes annoyance to all who witness it. Avoid all boastings and exaggerations, backand oaths in conversation ; depreciate no þÿman s would be amply paid for hy the shadow biting, abuse, and evil speaking ; slang phrases qualities, and accept hospitalities of the hum-

blest kind in a hearty and appreciative manner; avoid giving offence, and if you do offend, have the manliness to apologise ; infuse as much elegance as possible into your thoughts as well as your actions ; and as you avoid vulgarities you will increase the enjoyment of life, and grow in the respect of others.

Whispering is often indulged in by the young ; and my parting advice to all is, never to whisper, either in the presence or absence of others. What you cannot say plainly do not say at all ; and by never indulging in the practice you will never give way to it unconsciously in the presence of those who may think you are whispering of them.

The quarrel with Switzerland, which has been raised hy the King of Prussia in consequence of the abortive insurrection of his hotheaded friends in the canton of Neufchatel, presents no difficulty that any man of common sense and honesty could not equitably settle in five minutes. But the obstinacy ofthe King of Prussia and the stupidity ofthe Emperor ofthe French þÿ or of those persons who make use of the Moniteur in his name þÿ hid fair to surround this single question with endless exasperation and entanglements. The ultimate result may be the disturbance ofthe peace of Europe. The present result is a state of uncertainty and disquiet, and preparations for war that are almost as costly as war itself. The personal rights claimed by the King of Prussia over the canton of Neufchatel are not in dispute. The political rights of his Majesty, shadowy in the extreme, might, alter proper appraisement, he purchased from him by Switzerland without derogation of dignity- To the thinking of many they

of a live-franc piece. But whatever their worth þÿ and no one, however much inclined to take the part ofthe King of Prussia, values them at more than a merely nominal sum þÿ it is disgraceful and monstrous that a Sovereign who, during the war against Russia, would not stir a finger in defence of a cause which he admitted to be rightful, should, tor a trumpery point of supposed selfinterest on which the verdict of the world is against him, raise armies, put them in motion, and threaten a general disruption of Europe. When there was a great and a just war to be fought out, the King of Prussia was the þÿ Angel of þÿPeace. When peace is declared, and a question arises in which his own selflove is involved, the Angel of Peace is Adapt your greetings j transformed into the Demon ot Discord; and, for the paltry objects he expects to gain in a small corner of a small Republic, becomes as fi'-rce, as reckless, as insatiable as Nicholas was in pursuit of the prize of Constantinople. Frederick William will listen to no terms consent of compromise, unless Switzerland Count to abandon the trial of will

who, in his interest, if not at his instigation, took up arms, committed treason against the Republic, and murdered unoffending Swiss citizens. Switzerland cannot yield upon this point without a sacrifice of her independence and dignity. The point is vital. To abdicate her function as judge in the case of rebels against her authority would be to commit political suicide. The weaker she is in men and in money the more jealously she ought to maintain her indefeasible rights. It is hy her legality, far more than by her strength, that she exists in Europe, and that her independence is guaranteed to her by the consent, and by the express stipulation and solemn compact, ofthe Powers. But it is the conduct of France far more than that of Prussia which has complicated the question. Prussia, unaided and uncounselled, would not have dared, however much she might have talked and intrigued against Switzerland, to have attacked her with an armv. But, supported by France, there

is no knowing what folly or wickedness the King might not commit in pursuit of his visionary claims on Neufchatel. It is, therefore, to be hoped that the French Emperor will see the error which he has either committed iri his own per son or allowed others to commit in his name, and, without favour or prejudice, lend himself to the settlement of the dispute. If it had not been for the independence of Switzerland, which Switzerland knew how to maintain, amid difficulties quite as great as those which now menace her, the mighty Empen ofthe French might never have becon an Emperor, or even a President, or anything but an exile. He cannot p his hand upon his heart, if he still haone, and deny that hut for the gt nero aid which Switzerland afforded him ; the day of his adversity he might perhaps have ended his troubled career on that public place where other conspirators against strong and established Governments have so often displayed their heroism, or entitled themselves to he enrolled among the martyrs of liberty. If any one owe Switzerland a debt of gratitude it is Napoleon III.; hut, as the gratitude of Princes is even more phantasmal and shadowy than the rights of Prussia over Neufchatel, it is to the good. offices of Great Britain rather than to those of France that Switzerland and Europe will look to muzzle the warlike Sovereign of Berlin, and hind him over to keep the peace, of which he was once, and very lately, so doatingly enamoured. We do not imagine that

the personal relations already established, and about to he still more inti inately cemented, between the Rovai families of Windsor and Potsdam will form any impediment to the action of the British Government in the matter. It was the Premier of England who once insisted þÿ when he was not a Premier þÿ that nations had no cousins; and lie is not a likely person to forget at the pre- I sent time that cousins are not the only relatives of which nations are happily unconscious; that they neither marry nor are given in marriage; and that their only durable or valid alliances an those founded upon political necessitie. The King of Prussia is moving his armies towards the Swiss frontiers, and is said to have secured the consent ot the petty Sovereigns of Bavaria and Baden to a military passage through their territories- If so, Great Britain has only to declare such an attack upon Switzerland to he a catui belli, and the King of Prussia will become prudent and peaceable. In such a declaration, if rendered necessary, I ranee, not withstanding the opinion expressed in the Monit ur, would he certain to join. The Moniteur may detest freedom in Belgium, and coerce the Belgian press; it may detest freedom in England, and vainly threaten, because it cannot coerce, the English press; and it may also detest freedom in Switzerland and denounce the jealous care ofthe Swiss to guard inviolate the precious heirloom of their independence; hut, notwithstanding all these things, the Emperor of the French

will not allow the outbreak of a new war in Europe, to please the morbid vanity or exaggerated susceptibility of the King of Prussia, or any other potentate. Ugly, therefore, as it looks, we suspect that means will he found to put out the fire which has been kindled at Berlin, and that the Swiss difficulty will be allowed to blow over

COMMUNICATIONS. To the Editor of the þÿ þÿAvis. In some of the iate Nos. of the St. Croix Avis (9th and 13th Jany.), there are strictures on the new Postal Laws.

s x\ a $ o ij x a v i , In all other Governments the Post Office furnishes conveyances for the Mails or it cannot demand payment. Here in spite of Government furnishing no mail-boat expressly for the service þÿ in spite of the þÿKing packet s being the most contemptible vessel that sails out of the two- Ports, possessing neither speed nor accommodation for passengers, although almost all the business and correspondence between this Island and St. Thomas is carried on by a very superior class of private vessels, all letters, accounts, invoices, &c., must pass through a Post Office which has no means of conveying them. If the Post Office were of any use it would require no compulsory laws to induce men to avail themselves of it. In spite of these notorious and undeniable facts, we are now, in the decline of the Islands, to be taxed on a free privilege which has existed ever since their settlement, viz., that of inter-communication without taxation, and that without any reasonable pretext, for Government instead of going to any additional expense for furthering the intercourse between the Islands has reduced the packet service to a rate that no owners of suitable vessels will accept. A dismal falling þÿoff from the prospects that were held out 3 or 4 years ago of a Steamer to the þÿ þÿFly ! As to the St. Thomas observations about the facility of evading the law, I lind them most absurd ; it is no objection to a postal law that it may be evaded by stratagem. The game may be said of every impost in the world, but no smug-

gler is fool enough to tell how he lands his goods. The number of letters that escape postage has nothing to do with the fact that vast numbers do not ; that the money received for those that pay is a clear gain. If you make a good haul of fish it is no matter that a few get out of your net. As to the statistics of the Post Office we have nothing to do with them. The internal Post is certainly a great convenience, the only objection to it is that the rate of postage is fixed at an amount which cannot he paid in the currency of the Island, i. c. 3 cents instead of two stivers ; one may buy a stamp for 2 stivers purporting to be worth 3 cents, but if one sends the letter to the Post i Office to he stamped it costs 3 stivers. All this confusion is made for a difference of £ of a cent between 2 stivers the old postage, and 3 cents the new. What the use of these stamps is I cannot conceive, the Postmaster must still stamp with his rings ; could he not as well stamp paid on the letter ? If a man were even to write post-paid on his letter, it could be no loss to the Office, as the letter would not be forwarded if he did not send the money. There can he no valid reason why a poor man who cannot conveniently he out of a sum to purchase a quantity of stamps at once should pay more postage, which should be at a fixed rate for all, nor any why the Office should he paid for affixing the stamp. COMMUNICATION. To the Editor of the þÿ Avis. A Step in the Right Direction.

We have read with much pleasure a Prospectus in the þÿ þÿAvis, having for its object the issue of a Weekly Journal, containing judgments, rendered by the Courts in these Islands. Although the subject-matter is of the last importance, as tending to disseminate a useful knowledge of what is deemed right by the third power of the State, we have, yet heard many arguments advanced to prove that the matter is not feasible. To refute some of these aigumcnts we have taken up our pen; and if no succeed in encouraging the timid, animating t lie indifferent, and rousing the hold, we will deem our efforts not in vain. We have hoard it advanced, that the publisher promises more than lie is able to perform, as access to the records will he denied to him. We would observe, in the first instance, that the Courts, according to law, arc to he held public ; no one can be prevented from being present when judgment is pronounced, and the

publisher or his agent can thus avail himself of this medium to take down in short hand the words of such judgments. Besides, the courtesy of the respective Judges no doubt will extend so far as to furnish the publisher with the necessary copy or extract on his paying the þÿ tixed fees. In the second place, we take it for granted, that the plan will be. approved of by Government, when we reflect, that the State as an imperishable society could not realize its object by mere ideas ; but this can only be accomplished by the concurrence of its members. It is thus the duty of the State to encourage all enterprizes tending to enlighten its citizens ; hence we find in the newspapers published throughout the civilized world judgments and opinions pronounced by the different tribunals. We have farther heard it advanced, that such a journal will be as ephemeral as the þÿ Official þÿGazette, published under the auspices of Government þÿ a work, the advent of which was hailed with great joy as purporting to instruct all classes in the laws and regulations of the land, and which although making its appearance like þÿangels visitsþÿ few and far between þÿ was yet welcome : but it appears to have died a premature death. But we would observe, that such a circumstance ought not to prevent us encouraging the journal in contemplation, for by subscribing thereto we will prove, that the disappearance of said gazette, as well as the proceedings of the Colonial Council of the last session, cannot

be brought home to us. Besides, considering the purport of said journal, to impart a knowledge of what is considered right or wrong by the Courts, the subject-matter claims our support, independent of all such considerations. Again we have heard it advanced, that such a journal can only be of service to the man of law. We would observe in answer thereto, that such a conclusion is fallacious in the main. The man of law is invariably present when judgment is pronounced, and although he cites precedents he yet founds his plea on the statute laws of the land. But as examples are more efficacious than precepts so is the wording of judgments, rendered by the tribunals, more intelligible than the quibbles, and jargon of the law to the uninitiated. We have, moreover, heard it advanced, that the listless apathy of the inhabitants of these Islands would be an insurmountable obstacle in the way ; it would prevent the carrying out of the object of this journal. But when we call to mind, that the subscription list of the þÿ Official þÿGazette obtained a large number of subscribers, we apprehend, that a judicious selection of judgments rendered by our Courts, published with due discretion, will meet with as great success as said periodical. Emanating from llio press, it is to be expected that every one who appreciates his moral and political worth will contribute his mite in support of an institution which, although fettered at present, eventually will be found þÿ and safety-valve ; for the liberty of the press our only sheet-anchor

is the language of the þÿnation. In conclusion, wo would say to the timid, be re-assured ; to the indill'erent, be not selfish ; to the bold, light out the. good fight ; and to the publisher, God speed. Y. Z.

We copy the following biographical sketch from þÿ þÿDagbladet, of the 6tli instant : George Carstensen was born on the 31st August, 181:2, in Algiers. Ills father held the office of Dant-li Consul-General at Morocco. In 1835-36 ho resided alternately in Spain and Morocco ; in 1836-37 m Algiers and Paris; in 1837-38 in llie United States, u htc In1 published, in Philadelphia, a Periodical, in French and English. He afterwards travelled in England, France, Spain and þÿI oitugal. Alter a short stay in Copenhagen, where lie, in þÿ Hilleriip and Ilorgaard, published connection with þÿPortefeuillen, he again visited Paris, where he likewise engaged in literary avocations. In 1841 lie tixed his residence in quently þÿ Copenhagen, where he published þÿ þÿN y þÿPortefeuille and D.msk þÿAlbum. þÿ Figaro, subse- While publishing those Journals, Carstcnsen arranged large festivities in the garden-grounds at Rosenborg Castle and In the Riding .School. The entire arrangements were ol so novel a character, and there being so great a difference between this kind of amusements

S T & G; 0 li A V li S and those to which the public were before accustomed, that the people wore in ecstacies and wore completely carried away. It consequently was not long before Carstensen resigned the pursuit of literature, for which field he had no particular calling, and turned his attention in this direction, where he evinced great talent, and for which he fully deserves public gratitude. On the 7th Apnl, 1843, be obtained a grant for establishing Tivoli. On the breaking out of the war in 1848, Carstensen enlisted as 2nd Lieutenant, and left for the West Indies in September that year as 1st Lieutenant, where ho resided until the close of 1853, when lie resigned with the rank of Captain. By the Royal mail steam-ship Canada, which arrived at Liverpool on Tuesday morning, we have news from New York to tho 31st ult., and by telegraph, via Halifax, to the 1st inst. The slavery question, under some form or other, still continues to engross public attention. The proposal lor the open revival of the slave trade docs not meet with much encouragement, but the high price of negroes lias given a great impetus to the clandestine traffic in Africans. The New York Tribune says, it is a matter of certainty that New York lias been for a number of years the centre of the trade in slaves between the coast of Africa and Cuba. Tho number of slavers dispatched from New York within tho last three years, though not easy to state with precision, did not fall short of twenty-five or thirty. But, though only one of the three vessels captured has been condemned, and only two out of forty-six persons held to answer convicted, the efforts of tlie United þÿStates District Attorney and Deputy Marshals appear to have been not entirely thrown away. A number of the most active participants in the traffic have been driven out of tho city, and several slave captains and persons who visited New York with the object of buying or of fitting up vessels. The Portuguese Consul lias been suspended from his functions on suspicion of complicity. A steam revenue-cutter has lalely been fitted out at New York for tho prevention of Filibustering and the slave trade. A bill is before the Arkansas Legislature to

compel all free uegross to leave the State, under penalty of immediate sale into slavery for life A bill allowing negroes, Indians, and mulattoes to give evidence in cases where white persons are parties has passed the Senate branch of the Iowa Legislature by a vote of 1!) to 18. A bill þÿ to encourage and promote þÿmatrimony lias been introduced into the Legislature of North Carolina. The South Carolina Legislature, before its adjournment (on the :20th December), an. ended the law relative to coloured seamen arriving in that port. Hereafter they are not to he imprisoned. They arc only required to remain on board their vessels, and shipmasters give bonds securing their obedience to the laws of the State. This is a step m the right direction. This barbarous law, hereby repealed, was a disgiace o the State, and a source of annoyance and trouble to all vessels visiting the port of Charleston with negro seamen on hoard. It is one of tlm new signs now thickening of the relaxation of that ferocious spirit which has till now characterised American slavery It appears that the Legislature also refused to act on the matter of the revival of the slave trade,, which was so uublushingly forced upon their attention by Governor Adams, and that he failed also of a re-election.
