For the St. Croix þÿ Avis. A Chapter on the Shaking of Hands,

Pope, somewhere says, that the proper study of mankind is man ; þÿ we may also add, that to a particular observer, there is not a more easy way of discriminating character than by the simple shaking of bands. This subject, as far as we can recollect, has been treated of before and with much humour by a Gentleman of Massachusetts, þÿ we forget bis name, þÿ but notwithstanding a considerable lapse of years, the impression which we received has not been altogether obliterated. The following methods of shaking bands we shall forthwith proceed to classify under the following bends, and we seriously recommend them to the notice of those persons who wish to arrive at the required knowledge of character as far as these members of the Body can illustrate them. Wc proceed to state some of the principal heads, viz. : 1. The hearty shake. 2. The pump-handle shake. 3. The upright shake. 4. The downright shake. 5. The horizontal shake. 6. The supercilious shake. 7. The doubtful shake. 8. The two-fingered shake. And the no shake at all, or, clasped hands. To give a proper analysis of these different shakes, wc shall proceed methodically to describe what they generally denote, and hope that our readers will treasure them properly in the arehieves of their memory, and duly profit thereby. 1st. The hearty shake is generally given, when two friends meet, after a long absence. It sometimes consists in one of the parties giving to tlie other his hand, and together shaking them with such violence that till the muscles
are called into play þÿ and sometimes to the serious detriment of the weaker party. It frequently happens that instead of one both hands

S T C R 0 t X, AVIS . are given, and the demonstrations on both sides are so strongly shown, that serious risk is run, a cither of the dislocation of the wrist or of the shoulder-joint of one or other of the parties. Two conclusions may he drawn by a spectator of these ebullitions of feeling tints manifested þÿ one, that the parties arc perfectly sincere ; and the other, that this disguise is necessary to .conceal doubt and insincerity. 2d. The pump-handle shake consists in both parties seizing hold of down shaking them up and each others hands and in a slow, solemned and measured manner. This kind of shake generally takes place among people of a sanctified or of a hypocritical character ; who, at the time of shaking, observe each other full in t lie eyes in the most serious manner, and is seldom attended by any excitation of the risible muscles þÿ these different symptoms evidently denote that said shaking is a matter not lightly to be thought of. 3d. The upright shake consists in the mutual raising of the clasped hands of the parties, and the keeping of them momentarily suspended ; afterwards allowing them leisurely to descend þÿ this is sometimes the result of surprize and sometimes of imperfect recognition. 4th. The downright shake very seldom consists of more than one shake, of the hands of the parties, which, after elevation, descend with a certain degrde of force, and there remain in a strong squeeze, sufficiently trying to one or other of the parties. This with certain people is an indication of strong affection, and is some-

times a mark of mutual esteem ; this method of shaking hands is more prevalent among Scotchmen than among other people. 5tli. The horizontal shake manifests itself by a violent swinging of the hands and arms from one side to another; it is sometimes an indication of heartiness, and more frequently of carelessness, and an uncertain and wavering disposition. 6th. The supercilious shake consists in one of the parties giving to the other his fore finger instead of his hand, and is a certain sign that lie either thinks himself superior in station to the other, or that his acquaintance with him is of such trifling importance, as to fie a matter of perfect indifference to him. This shake is also given, by one of the individuals with some, hesitation, much coldness, and more hauteur þÿ lie, at the same time, regarding the other full in the eye and from head to foot once or twice repeatedly. 7th. The doubtful shake is a shake where both of the parties eye each other suspiciously, giving their hands with slowness and much caution. In the gossip which ensues, matters are twice thought of before utterance is given þÿ each tries to circumvent and overreach the other þÿ there is no unnecessary waste of words þÿ each party silently calculates his strength, and measures that of his opponent. In these contests a great deal of soft sawder is made use of, not unfrequently a good portion of blarney ; þÿ when you meet with characters of this description, keep a sharp look out or you will

inevitably be taken in. 8th. The two-fingered shake is an improvement on the one-fingered one. It shews on the part of the giver that he has some degree of consideration, but no kind of cordiality for the recipient of his digits. In addition to the above there are various other kinds of shakes which a keen observer ought not to lose sight of, such as the sly, the pompous, and the obsequious shakes. The two latter are generally between persons of different stations or conditions of life ns may evidently lie perceived by the bearing of the parties themselves : the pompous conducting himself with an air of condescension, at the same time being fully impressed that he considers it as such, by his cringing and obsequious manner of receiving it. We might go on ad infinitum , but what we have already stated will be enough to manifest the extreme importance to -he attached to this universal mode of salutation. It is a study not lightly to be esteemed, and cannot fail to he of utility at the same time, that it gives food for reflection to an enquiring and investigating mind, and ultimately may add to his stock of knowledge regards as human nature. Important Maxims Keep good company or none. Never be idle. If your hands cannot be usefully employed, attend to the cultivation of your mind. Always speak the truth. Make lew promises. Live up to your engagements. Keep your own secrets, if you have any. When you speak to a person look him full in the face. Good company and good conversation are the very sinews ol virtue. Good character is above all things else. Your character cannot be essentially injured except by your own acts. Never speak evil of any one. If any one speaks evil of you, let your life be so that no one will believe him. Ever live (misfortune excepted) within your income. Make no haste to be rich, if you would prosper. Small and steady gains give competency with tranquility of mind. Never gamble. Avoid temptation, through fear you may not withstand it. Earn money before you spend it. Never run into debt, unless you see a way to get out again. Never borrow, if you can possibly avoid it. Do not marry until you are able to support a wife. Be just before you are generous. Keep yourself innocent, if you would be happy. Save when you are young to spend when you are old. Read over the above maxims at least once a week.

The Charms of Life There are a thousand things in this world to afflict and sadden þÿ but oh ! how many that are beautiful and good ! The world teems with beauty þÿ with objects that gladden the eye and warm the heart. We might be happy if we would. There are ills which we cannot escape þÿ the approach of disease and death, of misfortunes, and the sundering of earthly ties. Let friendship, charity, love, purity, and kindness, mark the intercourse between man and man. We are too selfish, as if the world was made for us alone. How much happier should we be were we to labour more earnestly to promote each þÿother s good. God has blessed us with a home which is not all dark. There is sunshine everywhere þÿ in the sky, upon the earth þÿ there would be in most hearts if we would look around us. The storms die away, and the bright sun shines out. Summer drops her tinted curtain upon the earth, which is very beautiful, even when autumn breathes her changing breath upon it. God reigns in Heaven. Murmur not at a creation so beautiful, and who can live happier than we ?

NEW AMERICAN STEAM BATTERY. The great iron war steamer, which is now constructing at lloboken tor the Government, being an object ot much interest, wo have been at considerable pains to collect reliable information in regard to her,

FEBRUAR, 1 8 5 7. Nr. 16. principally through the medium of our Washington correspondents; and, as it differs very materially from the statements recently made in various quarters, we give it to our readers. In 1S42 the late Mr. Robert L, Stevens first broached to the Government the subject of harbour defence by means of steam batteries of iron, which should be shot and shell proof, and in 1843 Congress, by a special Act, directed that the Navy Department should contract with him for such a vessel. In 1844 a contract was accordingly made with him by Mr. Mason, then Secretary of the Navy, under which Mr. Stevens commenced collecting materials and constructing the dry dock in which the vessel is now building. Mr. Stevens bound himself by this contract to construct a war steamer suitable for use in the waters of New York, from Sandy Hook upward. It was stipulated that she should be built of iron, that she should be shot and shell proof against ordnance then in use on ships of war, that she should have four engines, and be propelled by a submerged propeller which should give great speed. Her dimensions were to be not less than 259 feet in length and 49 feet beam, and her cost complete, including an armament of not less than six heavy guns, was not to exceed S5S7.099. For the faithful fulfilment of this contract the Government required and received from Mr. Stevens ample security, as it was further stipulated that payments should be made to him as he proceeded with the construction up to 8590,090, and that the remaining $87,000

should be paid when the ship was completed and received. Mr. Stevens encountered many difficulties in making his preliminary arrangements, and it was not until July, 1854, that the actual construction was commenced. Meantime he had decided, after more fully studying the subject, to increase the dimensions of the vessel very much. Instead of a length of 250 feet she is nearly 429 feet long, and her other dimensions are increased in proportion. Instead of four engines and one propeller, she has eight engines and two propellers. Her boilers are 10 in number, of large dimensions, and her power will be nearly equal to 9,090 horses. The vessel is in a very advanced state, and the machinery and boilers, and dependencies are all complete in place. Owing to her greatly increased dimensions beyond those stipulated for in the contract the cost will be much increased, but how much we are not able to state. The payments by the Government cannot exceed 8509,000 until the vessel is delivered and received, unless Congress should make further appropriations. þÿ American paper.

The late escapes of French prisoners from Cayenne show what men will risk and enduie for' personal liberty, 'i he account is given by certain of the convicts now resident safely in New Yoik, and a more daring attempt we never heard of They were 011 a small island. They had no means of building a vessel, and were apparently too closely watched to permit of any thing of the kind. Their only resource was to build rafts, and this they did. Three rafts were built of small tubs and a few planks secured with ropes, which the convicts manufactured in secret out of the bark of trees ; sails were manufactured from old blouses, shirts, and waistcoats stitched together Three of these rafts were made. On one raft were nine men, among whom was a brother of Pianori, the assassin lately executed for his ther raft were twenty men, and on a attempt on the life of Napoleon III. On third anofourteen. On such conveyances, without a compass and without any sufficient stock of food, did forty-three men, of whom only two were sailors, set out upon a voyage, in which all science, skill, and weather cannot give complete security against any one of the many dangers to which these prisoners were exposed. The smallest raft bearing nine men, started first. It threatened to come to pieces after the party had been about twelve hours afloat, some of the casks of which it was composed began to leak, and had to be. taken up and repaired. This almost sunk the rest, and to lighten it some of the party were towed over-

board, till the casks were made be effected, and " this operation was renewed water-tight ; but only a temporary repair could night and day." After being four days and nights at sea they landed 011 a Dutch settlement, hauled up their raft and repaired it more effectually than it could be repaired afloat. After a night's labour they put to sea, keeping in shore, so as to land in case of pursuit, and on the seventh day they landed again During the latter portion of this voyage they suffered fearfully from hunger and thirst 1 hey had taken from Cayenne water and unthrashed corn sufficient for three days. By eking this out, with a few small crabs which they caught, and, of course, ate raw, they contrived to make it last six days. On the fifth day their allowance was half an ear of corn and a single crab to each man ; on this day, too, their water fell short ; on the seventh day they were driven by thirst gusting. In the to shifts the night, however, they had early most horrible and dissome relief. A little rain fell, which they could only catch in their sail, and then sucked out of the patchwork. They also caught some crabs. Having landed, they resolved to proceed the rest of their way on foot, but the fearful sufferings of the last three days had told upon thein, and five of their party, among whom was Piannri, were unable to proceed. The two who had a little strength left, set out, promising to return with help as soon as possible. For five days they walked bare-footed
